facts.statement: Gojirasaurus is a theropod dinosaur named after the Japanese movie monster Godzilla.
facts.quote: Gojirasaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur named after the Japanese giant movie monster Godzilla.

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus lived during the Late Triassic Period and includes only one known species.
facts.quote: It lived in the Late Triassic Period, containing a single known species, Gojirasaurus quayi.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter named Gojirasaurus quayi in 1997 based on holotype specimen UCM 47221 found in Quay County, New Mexico.
facts.quote: Gojirasaurus quayi was described and named by Kenneth Carpenter in 1997 based on a partial skeleton, the holotype specimen UCM 47221, from Quay County, New Mexico.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in the Bull Canyon Formation of the Dockum Group in eastern New Mexico.
facts.quote: The specimen hails from purplish-grey mudstones of the Bull Canyon Formation (sometimes called the Cooper Canyon Formation), a major fossiliferous component of the Dockum Group in eastern New Mexico.

facts.statement: Fossils of Gojirasaurus date to approximately 212 million years ago during the early Revueltian stage.
facts.quote: The Revuelto Creek fossils were deposited in the earlier part of the Revueltian, close to around 212 million years ago.

facts.statement: The name Gojirasaurus combines the Japanese monster "Gojira" and the Greek word for lizard, meaning "Godzilla lizard".
facts.quote: The generic name Gojirasaurus is derived from the name of the giant Japanese movie monster "Gojira" (Godzilla) and the Greek word "sauros" (σαυρος) meaning "lizard"; thus, "Godzilla lizard".

facts.statement: The name references the dinosaur's relatively large size compared to other Triassic theropods.
facts.quote: Carpenter (1997) selected "Gojira" in reference to the relatively large size of this theropod, which exceeded that of its Triassic counterparts.

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus was one of the largest Triassic theropods, reaching 5.5 to 6 meters in length and weighing at least 150 kg.
facts.quote: Gojirasaurus is one of the largest theropods known from the Triassic Period, with an estimate total length of 5.5 - 6 m long and a weight of at least 150 kg.

facts.statement: Features of the pelvis and ankle suggest the holotype was an immature individual that could have grown larger in maturity.
facts.quote: Carpenter (1997) pointed to features of the pelvis and ankle suggesting that this was an immature individual, and could therefore have grown to even a larger size in maturity.

facts.statement: Later studies confirmed that Gojirasaurus possessed features indicating it was ontogenetically immature.
facts.quote: Christopher T. Griffin (2019) and Griffin and Nesbitt (2020) confirmed that Gojirasaurus possessed features indicative of ontogenetic immaturity.

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus is distinguished from its relative Coelophysis by having a more robust tibia.
facts.quote: According to Nesbitt et al. (2007), Gojirasaurus can be distinguished based on the fact that its tibia is more robust than that of its relative Coelophysis.

facts.statement: Rauhut (2003) proposed that taller neural spines on mid and posterior dorsal vertebrae distinguish Gojirasaurus from other coelophysoids.
facts.quote: Rauhut (2003) attempted to diagnose this genus based on the fact that the mid/posterior dorsal vertebrae had taller neural spines than those observed in other coelophysoids.

facts.statement: Carpenter (1997) formally classified Gojirasaurus within the superfamily Coelophysoidea.
facts.quote: The formal naming and description of Gojirasaurus by Carpenter (1997) firmly classified it within Coelophysoidea.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Gojirasaurus belongs among the coelophysids or within Averostriformes, a grade including Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: In some analyses, Gojirasaurus maintains its position among the coelophysids, but other studies instead bring it over to Averostriformes, the grade of theropods including Dilophosaurus that leads to Averostra.

facts.statement: Its classification suggests Gojirasaurus was a bipedal, terrestrial, and actively mobile carnivore.
facts.quote: Gojirasaurus's assignment to the Coelophysoidea would suggest that it was a bipedal, terrestrial, actively mobile carnivore.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate about how much of the fossil material actually belongs to a single species.
facts.quote: A persistent question regarding Gojirasaurus quayi is how much of its fossil material actually belongs to one species.

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus is classified within the infraorder Coelophysoidea.
facts.quote: infraordo: Coelophysoidea

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus is classified within the family Coelophysidae.
facts.quote: familia: Coelophysidae

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus lived in North America during the Late Triassic, approximately 218 to 211 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Triásico, hace aproximadamente 218 y 211 millones de años, en el Noriense, en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus had a tibia measuring 469 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: El tamaño de su tibia era de 469 milímetros

facts.statement: The known specimen of Gojirasaurus was a juvenile measuring 5.5 meters long and weighing approximately 150 to 200 kilograms.
facts.quote: El espécimen es un juvenil de 5,5 metros y con un peso aproximado de 150 a 200 kilogramos

facts.statement: Adult Gojirasaurus could have reached a length of 6.5 meters.
facts.quote: Un adulto pudo haber medido 6,5 metros

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus is likely the largest carnivore of the Triassic period.
facts.quote: Gojirasaurus es probablemente el carnívoro más grande del periodo Triásico

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus had a larger spine than other coelophysids, possessed a long tail, and was bipedal.
facts.quote: tenía una espina dorsal más grande que otros celofisidos, tenía una larga cola y era bípedo

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus fossils were found in the Cañón Toro Formation, part of the Dockum Group, in Revuelto Creek, Quay County, New Mexico, USA.
facts.quote: Encontrado en la Formación Cañón Toro, parte del Grupo Dockum en Revuelto Creek, Quay Country, Nuevo México, Estados Unidos

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, known as UCM 47221, is a partial skeleton consisting of teeth, four ribs, and four vertebrae.
facts.quote: El espécimen es un esqueleto parcial representado por unos dientes, 4 costillas y 4 vértebras, se conoce como UCM 47221

facts.statement: Carpenter officially named and described the species as Gojirasaurus quayi, classifying it as a coelophysid.
facts.quote: Fue nombrada y descrita finalmente en forma oficial como Gojirasaurus quayi como un celofísido por Carpenter

facts.statement: Nesbitt et al. published in 2007 that the remains constitute a chimera, mixing bones from different animals.
facts.quote: Nesbitt et al. encuentran a los restos como una quimera, que fue elaborado en su publicación de 2007

facts.statement: The name Gojirasaurus references the 1954 Japanese film Gojira, known in the West as Godzilla.
facts.quote: El nombre hace referencia a Gojira película japonesa de 1954, que en occidente se llamó Godzilla

facts.statement: The specific name 'quayi' refers to Quay County, New Mexico, where the holotype specimen was discovered in 1997.
facts.quote: El nombre específico "quayi" es una referencia al condado de Quay, Nuevo México, donde se descubrió el espécimen holotipo en 1997

facts.statement: In 1997, Carpenter classified Gojirasaurus quayi within the family Coelophysidae.
facts.quote: Carpenter describió y nombró oficialmente UCM 47221, Gojirasaurus quayi en 1997 y lo clasificó como Coelophysidae

facts.statement: A 2007 study by Nesbitt et al. suggested the vertebrae belonged to the rauisuchian Shuvosaurus while the pubis and tibia belonged to a Coelophysid.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, un estudio posterior de Nesbitt et al. en 2007 demostró que las vértebras pertenecían realmente al rauisuchiano Shuvosaurus, y el pubis y la tibia pertenecían a un Coelophysidae

facts.statement: Rauhut attempted to diagnose the genus in 2003 based on higher neural spines on dorsal vertebrae compared to other coelophysids.
facts.quote: Rauhut en 2003 intentó diagnosticar este género basándose en el hecho de que las vértebras dorsales medias y posteriores tenían espinas neurales más altas que las observadas en otros celofísidos

facts.statement: Gojirasaurus lived during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, approximately 228 to 208 million years ago.
facts.quote: Este género se descubrió en 1981, en la piedra de barro carbonosa gris depositada durante la etapa noriana del Triásico tardío, que, según la magnetostratigrafía, de aproximadamente de 228 a 208 millones de años

facts.statement: Assignment to Coelophysoidea suggests Gojirasaurus was a bipedal, terrestrial, actively mobile carnivore.
facts.quote: La asignación de Gojirasaurus a Coelophysoidea, sugeriría que era un carnívoro bípedo, terrestre, activamente móvil

facts.statement: Contemporaries of Gojirasaurus included the pseudosuchian Shuvosaurus and the phytosaurian Rutiodon.
facts.quote: Contemporáneos de Gojirasaurus incluía el pseudosuquio Shuvosaurus y el fitosauriano Rutiodon

facts.statement: It is debated whether the remains of Gojirasaurus represent a single animal or a chimera of mixed fossils.
facts.quote: Nesbitt et al. encuentran a los restos como una quimera

facts.statement: The validity of Gojirasaurus as a distinct genus is doubtful due to conflicting fossil assignments.
facts.quote: lo que hace dudoso el estatus de Gojirasaurus como género válido

facts.statement: Mortimer proposed in 2012 that the robust tibia might be related to size rather than being a unique evolutionary trait.
facts.quote: Mortimer en 2012 ha propuesto que la diferencia observada en el hueso de la pierna podría estar relacionada con el tamaño, y no una verdadera apomorfia

rejected.quote: Several studies regard Gojirasaurus as a "metataxon": a collection of fossils for which assignment to a single species can neither be proven nor disproven.
